map.A report of sales over a year, shown wit: A report of yearly sales, costs and the profit earned
map.Making the product in a plant for sale t: A plan showing how a firm will market its product
map.Delivering the product to buyers by road: A list of the firm's employees and their pay rates

rt: A report of assets, liabilities and owner's equity
rw: A balance sheet lists what the firm owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner's equity left over, all at a single date.

ww.A report of yearly sales, costs and the: This describes an income statement, which covers sales, costs and profit over a period; a balance sheet instead shows assets, liabilities and equity at one date.
ww.A plan showing how a firm will market it: A marketing plan sets out how a firm will promote and sell its product, but it is not a financial statement, so it cannot be a balance sheet.
ww.A list of the firm's employees and their: A list of employees and pay rates is a payroll record kept for staff, not a financial statement of what the firm owns and owes.

rt: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
rw: The accounting equation says everything a firm owns is financed by creditors or the owner, so Assets equal Liabilities plus Owner's Equity, and the sheet balances.

ww.Profit = Assets + Liabilities: Profit comes from revenue minus expenses, not from adding assets and liabilities, so this mixes a balance sheet idea with an income statement idea.
ww.Equity = Assets + Liabilities: Adding liabilities to assets gives a meaningless total; equity is what is left after liabilities are subtracted from assets, so this has the signs wrong.
ww.Assets = Revenue minus Expenses: Revenue minus expenses gives profit, which belongs on the income statement; assets are matched against liabilities and equity, not against revenue and expenses.

rw: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities, so $50,000 minus $20,000 leaves $30,000 as the owner's share of the business.

ww.$50,000: $50,000 is the total assets, not the owner's equity; the $20,000 owed to creditors must be subtracted before the owner's share is known.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 is the liabilities figure itself, which is what the firm owes, not what is left for the owner after paying those debts.
ww.$70,000: $70,000 comes from adding liabilities to assets ($50,000 + $20,000), but debts must be subtracted, so this overstates the owner's equity badly.

map.The business's competitors, who sell sim: A report of assets, liabilities and equity at one date
map.A list of employees: A list of staff and their pay rates
map.The business's employees and their famil: A schedule of loan payments owed to the bank

rt: A report of revenues and expenses showing profit or loss
rw: An income statement lists revenues and expenses for a period and shows the resulting profit or loss, which is why it is called the profit and loss report.

ww.A report of assets, liabilities and equi: This describes a balance sheet, a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at one date, whereas an income statement covers a period of time.
ww.A list of staff and their pay rates: A list of staff and pay rates is a payroll record; it does not show revenues, expenses or the profit the business earned.
ww.A schedule of loan payments owed to the: A loan payment schedule tracks debt repayments to a bank, which is only one small item and not the full revenue and expense report.

rw: Gross profit equals sales minus cost of goods sold, so $60,000 minus $36,000 leaves $24,000 earned on the goods before other expenses.

ww.$36,000: $36,000 is the cost of goods sold itself; gross profit is what remains after subtracting that cost from the $60,000 of sales.
ww.$60,000: $60,000 is the sales figure before any cost is taken out, so it is revenue, not the gross profit left over.
ww.$96,000: $96,000 comes from adding sales and cost ($60,000 + $36,000), but the cost has to be subtracted, so the answer is wrongly inflated.

rw: Selling price equals cost plus markup, so $40 plus $25 gives $65, the price that covers the item's cost and adds the planned markup.

ww.$40: $40 is only what the retailer paid for the item; with no markup added, the shop would earn nothing on the sale.
ww.$15: $15 comes from subtracting the cost from the markup ($40 minus $25), but the markup is added to the cost, so this is wrong.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 comes from multiplying $40 by $25, but a markup is added to the cost rather than multiplied, so the arithmetic is wrong.

rw: Forty percent of the $50 cost is $20, and adding it to the cost gives a selling price of $70.

ww.$50: $50 is just the cost; a 40% markup adds $20 more, so selling at cost would leave the retailer with no profit.
ww.$90: $90 treats the 40% as $40 and adds it to $50, but 40% of $50 is only $20, so this overstates the price.
ww.$20: $20 is the markup amount alone (40% of $50), not the selling price, which must also include the $50 cost.

map.Making products in a factory for the sho: A rise in price added to cost to set the selling price
map.Filing taxes with the state each year by: A fee charged by a bank for a loan
map.A tax: A tax paid to the state on each sale

rt: A reduction in the selling price of a product
rw: A markdown is a reduction from the original selling price, often used for sales or clearing old stock, so this is the right definition.

ww.A rise in price added to cost to set the: This describes a markup, which raises the price above cost; a markdown goes the other way and lowers the price already set.
ww.A fee charged by a bank for a loan: A fee charged for a loan is bank interest or a service charge, which has nothing to do with changing the price of a product.
ww.A tax paid to the state on each sale: A tax on each sale is a sales tax and is set by the state; a markdown is a price cut made by the seller.

rw: A 25% markdown takes $20 off ($80 x 0.25), and $80 minus $20 leaves a sale price of $60.

ww.$100: $100 comes from adding 25% of $80 ($20) to the price, which would be a markup, but a markdown lowers the price instead.
ww.$20: $20 is the amount of the discount, not the new price; the sale price is what remains after taking it off $80.
ww.$55: $55 treats the 25% as $25 and subtracts it from $80, but 25% of $80 is $20, so the price should be $60.

rw: Rent stays the same at $2,000 a month no matter how many loaves are baked, which is the definition of a fixed cost.

ww.Profit: Profit is revenue minus costs, and rent is one of those costs, so rent cannot be profit.
ww.Variable cost: A variable cost changes with output, but rent stays at $2,000 whether the bakery bakes many loaves or none, so it is not variable.
ww.Revenue: Revenue is money earned from sales, while rent is money paid out, so rent is a cost and cannot be revenue.

rt: Variable cost
rw: Flour is used up more as more loaves are baked, so its total cost rises with output, which makes it a variable cost.

ww.Revenue: Revenue is money coming in from sales, but flour is an input the bakery pays for, so it is a cost, not revenue.
ww.Fixed cost: A fixed cost stays the same at any output, but flour use rises with each extra loaf, so flour is not fixed.
ww.Profit: Profit is what remains after costs are subtracted from revenue, so flour, which is one of those costs, is not profit.

rt: Fixed costs plus variable costs
rw: Total cost is fixed costs plus variable costs, covering everything the firm pays whether or not output changes.

ww.Variable costs only: Variable costs alone leave out costs like rent that do not change with output, so they are only part of the total cost.
ww.Fixed costs only: Fixed costs alone leave out materials and other costs that change with output, so they are only part of the total cost.
ww.Revenue minus expenses: Revenue minus expenses gives profit, not cost, so this describes the firm's earnings and not what it spent in total.

rw: Variable cost is 1,500 x $2 = $3,000, and adding the $3,000 fixed cost gives a total cost of $6,000.

ww.$7,500: $7,500 is $3,000 plus $5 per cup, but the variable cost is $2 per cup, so the right sum is $3,000 plus $3,000.
ww.$4,500: $4,500 adds the 1,500 cups to the $3,000 fixed cost, but variable cost is $2 per cup, so 1,500 x $2 = $3,000 must be added.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the fixed cost only; it leaves out the variable cost of 1,500 cups at $2 each, which adds another $3,000.

rw: Average cost per cup is total cost divided by cups, so $6,000 / 1,500 = $4 per cup.

ww.$6: $6 would be right only for 1,000 cups ($6,000 / 1,000); the question gives 1,500 cups, so the division is wrong.
ww.$9,000: $9,000 comes from multiplying $6,000 by 1.5, but average cost needs division by the 1,500 cups, not multiplication.
ww.$2: $2 is far too low; $2 x 1,500 cups is only $3,000, which would be half of the stated $6,000 total cost.

rw: Profit per cup equals price minus cost per cup, so $5 minus $4 leaves $1 earned on each cup sold.

ww.$9: $9 comes from adding the price and the cost ($5 + $4), but profit needs the cost subtracted from the price.
ww.$4: $4 is the cost of each cup, not the profit; profit is what remains of the $5 price after that cost.
ww.$20: $20 comes from multiplying $5 by $4, but profit per unit is found by subtracting cost from price, not multiplying them.

rw: Each unit contributes $15 minus $9 = $6 toward fixed costs, so break-even is $1,800 / $6 = 300 units.

ww.1,800 units: 1,800 units would only be right if each unit earned $1; here each unit contributes $6, so far fewer sales are needed.
ww.120 units: 120 units comes from dividing $1,800 by the $15 price, but break-even must divide by the $6 contribution margin.
ww.200 units: 200 units comes from dividing $1,800 by the $9 variable cost, but the divisor should be the $6 contribution margin.

map.More customers than the store needs in p: Selling price plus fixed cost per unit
map.Lower storage costs for the store: Fixed cost divided by the units sold

rw: Contribution margin per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit, the amount each sale adds toward covering fixed costs.

ww.Selling price plus fixed cost per unit: Adding fixed cost per unit to the price is not a margin; contribution margin subtracts variable cost from the selling price, so this has the wrong inputs.
ww.Fixed cost divided by the units sold: Fixed cost divided by units sold is fixed cost per unit, which says nothing about how much each sale contributes after variable costs.
ww.Total revenue minus total cost: Total revenue minus total cost is the overall profit for all units, not the per-unit amount left after variable costs are paid.

map.Output falls to zero immediately: Output always rises faster as inputs are added
map.Making goods in a plant from raw materia: Costs fall forever as output rises
map.Counting goods in the stockroom daily: Output never changes as inputs rise

rt: Extra inputs add less and less extra output
rw: The law of diminishing returns says that after some point each added unit of input brings a smaller gain in output.

ww.Output always rises faster as inputs are: This says the opposite of the law; adding more inputs does not always speed up output, and gains eventually become smaller.
ww.Costs fall forever as output rises: Costs do not fall forever as output rises; with diminishing returns, extra output eventually becomes more costly to produce.
ww.Output never changes as inputs rise: Output usually does rise when inputs rise, just by smaller amounts, so saying it never changes is incorrect.

rt: Lower average cost as output grows
rw: Economies of scale means average cost per unit falls as a firm grows its output, because fixed costs are spread over more units.

map.Weighing items: Higher average cost as output grows
map.A manager of a store or shop: A fixed price set for all goods
map.Selling fewer goods: Selling fewer goods at higher prices

ww.Higher average cost as output grows: Higher average cost with growth describes diseconomies of scale, the opposite of the idea, where a firm becomes too big to run well.
ww.A fixed price set for all goods: Economies of scale concerns average cost falling as output grows, not a fixed price set for all goods by anyone.
ww.Selling fewer goods at higher prices: Selling fewer goods would raise the average cost per unit because fixed costs are spread over fewer sales, which is the opposite.

map.Replacing all employees with machines, s: The total cost of producing all units made
map.Removing the need for customers by makin: The cost per unit averaged over all units
map.Guaranteeing profit for every firm that: The fixed cost that stays the same at any output

rw: Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit, found as the change in total cost from adding that unit.

ww.The total cost of producing all units ma: The total cost of all units made is total cost, not marginal cost, which looks only at the added cost of one more unit.
ww.The cost per unit averaged over all unit: Cost per unit averaged over all units is average cost; marginal cost looks only at the one additional unit being added.
ww.The fixed cost that stays the same at an: Fixed cost stays the same at any output, so the extra cost of one more unit would not include it.

rt: Extra revenue from selling one more unit
rw: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue earned from selling one more unit, found as the change in total revenue.

map.A restaurant removing its phone so peopl: Extra cost of producing one more unit
map.A restaurant closing early on busy night: Revenue per unit averaged over all sales

ww.Extra cost of producing one more unit: The extra cost of one more unit is marginal cost, which is compared with marginal revenue but is a different measure.
ww.Total revenue minus total cost: Total revenue minus total cost is profit, a total for all units, not the extra revenue from one added unit.
ww.Revenue per unit averaged over all sales: Revenue per unit averaged over all sales is average revenue, which differs from the extra revenue earned on one more unit.

map.Never: When marginal cost is above marginal revenue
map.Business done only in one town, with no: Only when fixed costs fall to zero for the firm
map.Business done without customers or buyer: Whenever total cost is lower than last year

rt: While marginal revenue is above marginal cost
rw: A firm should raise output while each extra unit brings in more revenue than it costs, meaning marginal revenue is above marginal cost.

ww.When marginal cost is above marginal rev: If marginal cost is above marginal revenue, each added unit loses money, so a firm following marginal analysis should cut output.
ww.Only when fixed costs fall to zero for t: Fixed costs do not change with output, so they are ignored by marginal analysis; the decision turns on marginal revenue and marginal cost.
ww.Whenever total cost is lower than last y: Lower total cost than last year is a comparison across time, not the marginal test of added revenue against added cost.

map.A cost such as rent that stays the same: A cost such as rent that stays fixed at any output
map.A tax on exports alone: A shared overhead like office lighting for all products
map.A ban on trade in goods: A tax charged on the final sale price

rw: A direct cost can be traced straight to a specific product, as raw materials can, which makes this the correct definition.

ww.A cost such as rent that stays fixed at: Rent that stays fixed at any output is a fixed cost, which is often indirect; a direct cost is traced to a particular product.
ww.A shared overhead like office lighting f: A shared overhead such as office lighting cannot be traced to one product, so it is an indirect cost, not a direct one.
ww.A tax charged on the final sale price: A tax on the final sale price is not a cost traceable to producing a product, so it is not a direct cost.

map.A volunteer role with no pay at all: The increase in an asset's value over time
map.A hobby done for fun at home daily: The cash a firm owes to its suppliers
map.A tax: A tax on the profit of a firm

rw: Depreciation spreads the falling value of an asset, such as a machine or truck, over its useful life due to wear or age.

ww.The increase in an asset's value over ti: Depreciation is a decrease, not an increase; a rise in an asset's value would be appreciation, so this is the opposite.
ww.The cash a firm owes to its suppliers: Cash owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability, not the loss of value of an asset over time.
ww.A tax on the profit of a firm: A tax on profit is an expense paid to the government and is unrelated to an asset losing value through use or age.

map.A career is unpaid, while a job is paid: A measure of cost relative to sales revenue
map.A job lasts for life, while a career las: The total amount an owner puts into a firm
map.They mean exactly the same thing in all: The tax paid on investment income

rw: ROI measures profit relative to the amount invested, usually shown as a percentage, so it tells an owner how well the money worked.

ww.A measure of cost relative to sales reve: Cost relative to sales revenue is not ROI; return on investment compares the profit earned with the money put into the venture.
ww.The total amount an owner puts into a fi: The total an owner puts in is the investment, which is only the bottom of the ROI fraction and not the ratio itself.
ww.The tax paid on investment income: Tax on investment income is a cost to the investor, not a measure of how much profit an investment earned.

rw: ROI equals profit divided by investment, so $1,500 / $10,000 = 0.15, or 15%, the return earned on the owner's money.

ww.6.7%: 6.7% comes from inverting the fraction, as $10,000 / $1,500 is about 6.67; ROI divides profit by investment, giving $1,500 / $10,000.
ww.$11,500: $11,500 adds the profit to the investment ($10,000 + $1,500), a dollar total, whereas ROI is a percentage ratio of profit to investment.
ww.150%: 150% moves the decimal wrongly; $1,500 / $10,000 = 0.15, which is 15%, not 150%.

map.A tax rate: Total cost divided by units produced
map.Choosing the job with the shortest title: Fixed cost as a share of total cost
map.Choosing a job at random from a list of: Sales revenue as a percentage of total cost

rt: Net profit as a percentage of sales
rw: A profit margin is net profit as a percentage of sales, showing how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit.

ww.Total cost divided by units produced: Total cost divided by units produced is average cost per unit, not a margin, which compares profit with sales revenue.
ww.Fixed cost as a share of total cost: Fixed cost as a share of total cost shows the cost structure, but it says nothing about how much profit each sale earns.
ww.Sales revenue as a percentage of total c: Revenue as a percentage of cost compares sales with spending and has the ratio upside down; a margin divides profit by revenue.

rw: Profit margin is net profit divided by sales, so $16,000 / $200,000 = 0.08, or 8%, the profit kept from each sales dollar.

ww.12.5%: 12.5% is $200,000 / $16,000 = 12.5, which inverts the fraction; the profit should be the top number and the sales the bottom.
ww.0.8%: 0.8% puts the decimal one place too far to the left; $16,000 / $200,000 is 0.08, which is 8%, not 0.8%.
ww.80%: 80% misplaces the decimal in the other direction; $16,000 is a small share of $200,000, so the margin is 8%, not 80%.

rt: What to produce, how to produce and for whom
rw: Every society has scarce resources, so it must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, the three basic questions.

map.It removes the need to learn new skills: Where to build roads, schools and parks only
map.It lets you avoid all of your weaknesses: Which currency to use and which bank to trust

ww.Where to build roads, schools and parks: Where to build roads, schools and parks is just a planning detail; it is not the basic set of three questions about production.
ww.Who to tax, who to hire and who to fire: Who to tax, hire and fire are management and government decisions, not the basic questions of what, how and for whom to produce.
ww.Which currency to use and which bank to: Which currency or bank to use is a money matter; the basic questions concern what, how and for whom to produce.

map.A salary level paid by a firm to staff: An economy where private firms make every decision
map.A required degree that a worker must hol: An economy run by custom and tradition alone
map.A job title printed on a business card: An economy with no trade between countries

rw: In a command economy the government makes major decisions about what is produced, how and for whom, instead of markets deciding.

ww.An economy where private firms make ever: An economy where private firms make every decision is a market economy, the opposite of a command economy run by government.
ww.An economy run by custom and tradition a: An economy run by custom and tradition alone is a traditional economy, not a command economy, where government makes the big decisions.
ww.An economy with no trade between countri: An economy with no trade between countries is called a closed economy, which describes trade, not who makes economic decisions.

map.A salary history listing the pay of your: A system where the market alone sets all prices
map.A system of private ownership: A system of private ownership of all firms
map.A view from a window at work, showing th: A system run by tradition and custom

rt: A system where the state owns key industries
rw: Socialism is a system in which the state or community owns key industries and resources, in place of private owners.

ww.A system where the market alone sets all: A system where the market alone sets all prices is a market economy or capitalism, not socialism, which gives the state a large role.
ww.A system of private ownership of all fir: Private ownership of all firms describes capitalism; socialism rests on public or collective ownership of important industries.
ww.A system run by tradition and custom: A system run by tradition and custom is a traditional economy, not socialism, which relies on public ownership and planning.

map.An advertisement for a job or a firm in: Government decides what firms must produce
map.Prices are fixed: Prices are fixed by law for all goods
map.An anonymous social media post that clai: Firms decide what to make without regard to buyers

rt: Consumer buying choices decide what firms produce
rw: Consumer sovereignty means buyers' choices decide what firms produce, since firms that fail to satisfy shoppers lose sales and profit.

ww.Government decides what firms must produ: Government deciding what firms must produce describes a command economy; consumer sovereignty gives that power to buyers.
ww.Prices are fixed by law for all goods: Prices fixed by law for all goods describes price controls, not consumer sovereignty, where shoppers' choices guide what is made.
ww.Firms decide what to make without regard: Firms ignoring buyers is the reverse of consumer sovereignty, where producers must respond to what consumers choose to buy.

map.A person who hires employees for a firm: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
map.A person who sells products to buyers in: Price has no effect on the quantity bought
map.Demand never changes: As price falls, quantity supplied rises

rt: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
rw: The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price means buyers purchase a smaller quantity, so demand slopes downward.

ww.As price rises, quantity demanded rises: Quantity demanded does not rise as price rises; this is the opposite of the law of demand, where higher prices cut buying.
ww.Price has no effect on the quantity boug: Price has a clear effect on how much is bought, which is exactly what the law of demand describes.
ww.As price falls, quantity supplied rises: As price falls, quantity supplied rises is not the law of demand; supply and demand are different, and sellers respond to prices differently.

map.Supply never changes: Supply is unaffected by price changes
map.A list of stocks you own in a firm or in: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
map.A record of your spending kept in a book: As price rises, quantity demanded falls

rt: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
rw: The law of supply says that, other things equal, a higher price leads producers to offer a larger quantity for sale.

ww.Supply is unaffected by price changes: Supply responds to price, so claiming it is unaffected is incorrect; the law of supply says it rises with price.
ww.As price rises, quantity supplied falls: Quantity supplied falls as price rises would reverse the law; higher prices give sellers more incentive to produce, not less.
ww.As price rises, quantity demanded falls: Quantity demanded falling as price rises is the law of demand, which describes buyers, not the law of supply for sellers.

rw: At a price above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus occurs.

ww.Demand rises: A price above equilibrium makes buyers want less, not more, so demand does not rise; the result is a surplus.
ww.Equilibrium occurs: Equilibrium is the price where supply meets demand, and a price above it is by definition not equilibrium.
ww.A shortage occurs: A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium and buyers want more than sellers offer; a high price does the reverse.

rt: A shortage occurs
rw: When the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers supply, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage occurs.

ww.A surplus occurs: A surplus happens when the price is above equilibrium; a price below it leaves buyers wanting more than sellers offer.
ww.Prices fall further: Prices would tend to rise, not fall, when there is a shortage, so saying that they fall further is backwards.
ww.Equilibrium occurs: Equilibrium is the price where the market clears, and a price below it is by definition not at equilibrium.

rw: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price set by government, which sellers cannot charge above, as in rent control.

ww.A legal minimum price: A legal minimum price is a price floor, not a ceiling; a ceiling sets the highest price that sellers may charge.
ww.A tax on imported goods: A tax on imported goods is a tariff, a trade measure that is unrelated to a legal limit on price.
ww.A subsidy paid to producers: A subsidy is money paid to producers to lower costs, not a legal limit on how high a price may go.

map.Only one printed newspaper in your own h: A price set by the seller alone

rt: A legal minimum price
rw: A price floor is a legal minimum price that cannot be charged below, such as a minimum wage set by the government.

ww.A tax on imported goods: A tax on imported goods is a tariff and does not set a lowest legal price for any product.
ww.A price set by the seller alone: A price set by the seller alone is not a government rule, whereas a price floor is a legal limit set by authorities.
ww.A legal maximum price: A legal maximum price is a price ceiling, which is the opposite of a floor that stops prices from falling below a set level.

rw: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period, usually a year.

map.Your friends' names and their phone numb: The total tax collected by a government in a year
map.Your passwords and your bank account num: The total money a government owes to lenders
map.Your favorite foods and your favorite sh: The total value of goods a country imports

ww.The total tax collected by a government: Tax revenue collected by a government is only one small item in a nation's finances and does not measure total production.
ww.The total money a government owes to len: Money owed to lenders is national debt, which measures what the government owes, not the value of goods and services produced.
ww.The total value of goods a country impor: The value of imported goods counts trade only and leaves out most of what a country produces, so it is not GDP.

map.A list of games played, with scores and: Central bank control of interest rates and money supply
map.Consumer budgeting: A firm's plan for hiring and pay
map.Made-up jobs that you never held at any: Rules limiting how much a country may import

rt: Government use of taxes and spending to guide the economy
rw: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxes and spending to influence growth, jobs and prices in the economy.

ww.Central bank control of interest rates a: Central bank control of interest rates and the money supply is monetary policy, not fiscal policy, which belongs to the government.
ww.A firm's plan for hiring and pay: A firm's plan for hiring and pay is a business decision, not a national policy tool for managing the whole economy.
ww.Rules limiting how much a country may im: Rules that limit imports are trade policy, which affects foreign trade, not the taxing and spending of fiscal policy.

map.To make it longer than a single page: Rules that limit imports of goods
map.Household budgeting: A family's plan for saving money

rt: Central bank control of money supply and interest rates
rw: Monetary policy is the central bank's control of the money supply and interest rates to steer inflation and growth.

ww.Government taxes and spending choices: Government taxes and spending choices are fiscal policy; monetary policy is run by the central bank, not by the government's budget.
ww.Rules that limit imports of goods: Rules that limit imports are trade policy and have nothing to do with the supply of money or interest rates.
ww.A family's plan for saving money: A family's plan for saving money is household budgeting, which works at home and does not set money supply for the nation.

rt: The central bank of the United States
rw: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, which sets monetary policy and oversees banks across the country.

map.Writing a draft quickly in one sitting: The agency that collects federal income taxes
map.A commercial bank that lends to firms an: A commercial bank that lends to firms for profit
map.Printing a document on paper for use: A stock exchange where shares are traded

ww.The agency that collects federal income: The agency that collects federal income taxes is the Internal Revenue Service, a different body from the Federal Reserve.
ww.A commercial bank that lends to firms fo: The Fed is not a commercial bank that lends to firms for profit; it is the central bank that serves banks and the government.
ww.A stock exchange where shares are traded: A stock exchange is a market where shares are traded, while the Federal Reserve runs monetary policy and supervises banks.

rw: A quota sets a maximum quantity of a good that may be imported in a period, limiting supply from foreign producers.

ww.A tax on imports: A tax on imports is a tariff, which raises the price of foreign goods but does not cap how many may enter.
ww.A price ceiling: A price ceiling limits how high a price may be set, which is a price control and not a limit on imports.
ww.A subsidy: A subsidy is money paid by government to producers, so it helps sellers and does not cap the quantity imported.

rw: A trade deficit occurs when a country buys more from abroad than it sells abroad, so imports are larger than exports.

ww.When there is no trade: When there is no trade, imports and exports are both zero, so this is not a deficit, which needs imports above exports.
ww.When trade is balanced: When trade is balanced, exports equal imports, so no deficit exists; a deficit requires imports to be larger.
ww.When exports exceed imports, so that the: Exports exceeding imports means the country sells more than it buys, which is a trade surplus and not a deficit.

rw: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than others do, so trade lets each side specialize and gain.

ww.Having the most resources: Having the most resources is absolute strength; comparative advantage depends on the lowest opportunity cost, not on resource size.
ww.Selling the most: Selling the most describes sales volume; comparative advantage is about giving up less of other goods when producing something.
ww.Making everything cheapest: Making everything cheapest is absolute advantage, and a country cannot hold comparative advantage in every good at once.

rw: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many dollars buy one euro.

ww.A bank fee: A bank fee is a charge for a service and has nothing to do with the price of one currency in another.
ww.A tax on money: A tax on money is not an exchange rate; the rate is a market price for swapping one currency for another.
ww.A loan rate: A loan rate is interest charged on borrowing, which differs from the rate at which currencies are swapped.

rw: A career pathway is a planned sequence of education, training and experience that leads toward a chosen career goal.

ww.A job application: A job application is a form sent to apply for a job, not a planned sequence of steps toward a career.
ww.A salary table: A salary table lists pay levels for jobs, which does not describe the education and experience needed to reach a career goal.
ww.A hallway: A hallway is a physical passage in a building and has nothing to do with a plan for building a career.

rw: Soft skills are interpersonal traits like communication, teamwork and adaptability that help workers succeed with others in any job.

ww.Math formulas: Math formulas are technical knowledge that can be taught and measured, so they are hard skills, not soft skills.
ww.Machine operation: Machine operation is a technical ability learned through training, which makes it a hard skill and not a soft skill.
ww.Technical computer skills: Technical computer skills are measurable and can be taught directly, so they count as hard skills, not people skills.

rw: Hard skills are teachable, measurable abilities such as coding or accounting that can be tested and listed on a resume.

ww.Friendliness: Friendliness is a personal trait that is hard to measure or test, so it is a soft skill, not a hard skill.
ww.Personality traits: Personality traits are part of who a person is and are not taught in a course, so they are soft skills.
ww.Teamwork: Teamwork is an interpersonal skill used with others and is hard to measure, so it is classed as a soft skill.

rw: A thank-you note after an interview expresses appreciation for the interviewer's time and reaffirms your interest in the job.

ww.Criticize the interview, and suggest way: Criticizing the interview would give a poor impression and could cost you the job; a thank-you note should be polite and positive.
ww.Demand a job: Demanding a job is rude and pushy; a thank-you note is a courteous message and is not a place for demands.
ww.Skip it: Skipping the note throws away a chance to stand out, because a short thank-you shows good manners and keeps you in mind.

rw: Career networking means building professional relationships that can lead to job leads, advice, references and other opportunities.

ww.Connecting computers: Connecting computers is computer networking, a technology activity, whereas career networking is about meeting and building contacts.
ww.Filing papers: Filing papers is office work and does nothing to build the relationships that can lead to job openings.
ww.Buying supplies: Buying supplies is a purchasing task and is unrelated to meeting people who can help your career.

rw: A professional reference is a person, such as a past boss or teacher, who can vouch for your skills and character.

ww.A job title that is printed on a busines: A job title on a business card names a role you hold; a reference is a person who speaks for you.
ww.A salary figure that an employer offers: A salary figure offered by an employer is a pay offer, not a person who can vouch for your skills.
ww.A book list that shows what an applicant: A book list is a record of reading and does not help an employer judge your work or character.

rw: A portfolio is a collection of work samples, such as writing or designs, that shows an employer what you can do.

ww.A bank account: A bank account holds money and does not show an employer what work you can do.
ww.A wallet: A wallet carries cash and cards; it is not a record of your work samples.
ww.A stock list: A stock list shows investments, which have nothing to do with demonstrating your skills to an employer.

rw: A personal brand is how you present yourself and what you are known for, including your skills, values and reputation at work.

ww.A product logo that a company prints on: A product logo identifies a company's goods on packaging and ads; a personal brand is about a person, not a product.
ww.A tax label that is added to a product w: A tax label added to goods sold abroad concerns trade rules and has no link to how a person presents themselves.
ww.A store name that appears on the sign ab: A store name on a sign identifies a shop and has nothing to do with how a person is seen professionally.

rw: A work ethic is a set of values built around hard work, reliability and responsibility, which employers prize in any role.

ww.A habit of blaming others whenever a pro: Blaming others when a project fails shows a lack of responsibility, which is the opposite of a strong work ethic.
ww.A habit of doing only the minimum that a: Doing only the minimum a manager accepts shows low effort, not the dedication and diligence a work ethic describes.
ww.A habit of avoiding tasks whenever someo: Avoiding tasks when others will do them shows a lack of responsibility, which is the reverse of a good work ethic.

rw: A job application gives employers information about your qualifications, such as education, experience and skills, so they can decide on an interview.

ww.To accept a job: You accept a job through an offer and reply, not through the application, which only asks to be considered.
ww.To request a loan: A loan is requested with a loan application, which is a separate document from one used to apply for a job.
ww.To pay taxes: Taxes are paid through tax forms and filings, which are not what a job application is meant for.

rw: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck, based on your filing details.

ww.Your vacation days: Vacation days are set by company policy or an employment agreement, not by the W-4 tax form.
ww.Your job title: Your job title is set by the employer when you are hired and does not come from the W-4.
ww.Your hourly wage: Your hourly wage is agreed with the employer at hiring; the W-4 only affects how much tax is withheld.

rw: The I-9 form lets an employer verify a new employee's identity and eligibility to work in the United States, using approved documents.

ww.Reporting taxes: Reporting taxes is done with tax forms like the W-4 and W-2, not with the I-9, which checks work eligibility.
ww.Reporting wages: Wages are reported on forms like the W-2 and not on the I-9, which concerns identity and work authorization.
ww.Choosing benefits: Choosing benefits is done in enrollment forms from the employer; the I-9 has no role in picking insurance or retirement plans.

rw: Gross pay is total earnings before taxes and other deductions are taken out, so it is the full amount a worker earned.

ww.Savings: Savings is money set aside from earnings and is not the same as what a worker earned before deductions.
ww.Tax owed: Tax owed is just one deduction from pay; gross pay is the total earnings before any deductions are made.
ww.Take-home pay, which is the sum left aft: Take-home pay is net pay, the amount left after deductions; gross pay is the larger figure before those are removed.

rw: Net pay is the pay remaining after taxes and other deductions are taken from gross pay, also called take-home pay.

ww.Tax withheld: Tax withheld is only one deduction taken from earnings, not the amount of pay that remains afterward.
ww.Total earnings before taxes and deductio: Total earnings before taxes and deductions are gross pay, which is larger than net pay because deductions are not yet removed.
ww.Bonus: A bonus is extra pay on top of regular earnings, and it is not the amount left after deductions.

rw: Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions, so $1,500 minus $330 leaves $1,170 as the worker's take-home pay.

ww.$330: $330 is the amount of deductions only, not what the worker takes home after they are removed from $1,500.
ww.$1,830: $1,830 adds the deductions to gross pay ($1,500 + $330), but deductions are taken away, so net pay must be lower.
ww.$1,500: $1,500 is the gross pay before any deductions, so it ignores the $330 that comes out of the paycheck.

rw: A salary is a fixed regular payment for work, usually stated as an annual amount and paid in equal installments.

ww.Pay per sale: Pay per sale is a commission, which varies with sales, whereas a salary stays fixed from one pay period to the next.
ww.A tip: A tip is a gift of money from a customer for service, not a regular payment from an employer.
ww.Pay per hour: Pay per hour is a wage, which depends on hours worked, while a salary is a fixed amount set for the year.

rw: A wage is pay based on the hours worked, so a worker earns an hourly rate multiplied by the hours on the job.

ww.A bonus: A bonus is extra pay on top of regular earnings, not the basic rate based on hours worked.
ww.Sales percentage: A sales percentage is a commission, which depends on how much the worker sells and not on hours.
ww.Annual fixed pay, which is paid in equal: Annual fixed pay in equal amounts is a salary, which does not change with hours, so it is not a wage.

rw: Gross weekly pay equals the hourly rate times the hours worked, so $14 x 35 = $490 before any deductions.

ww.$49: $49 adds the hourly rate and the hours ($14 + $35), but earnings come from multiplying the rate by the hours.
ww.$4,900: $4,900 puts the decimal two places too far; $14 x 35 hours is $490, not $4,900.
ww.$2.50: $2.50 comes from dividing hours by rate ($35 / $14), but gross pay is found by multiplying them.

rw: Researching the company and practicing answers shows interest and helps you give clear, confident replies to likely questions.

ww.Skip research: Skipping research leaves you unable to speak about the employer or the job, which hurts your chances in the interview.
ww.Arrive late: Arriving late gives a poor first impression and suggests you are unreliable, so it is not preparation of any kind.
ww.Wing it: Winging it leaves you unready for common questions and shows little effort, whereas preparing ahead builds confidence.

rw: Neat, professional attire shows respect for the employer and the interview, and it helps you make a good first impression.

ww.Beachwear: Beachwear is far too casual for a business interview and suggests you do not take the job seriously.
ww.Whatever is comfortable only: Dressing only for comfort could leave you too casual or untidy, and that gives a poor impression to an employer.
ww.Pajamas: Pajamas are for sleeping and are never suitable for an interview, which calls for neat, professional clothing.

rw: Asking what success looks like shows you want to do well and helps you learn what the employer expects from the role.

ww.How little can I do?: Asking how little you can do shows a poor work ethic and would likely end the interviewer's interest in you.
ww.How soon can I take my first vacation af: Asking about a vacation before you have an offer suggests you care more about time off than the job itself.
ww.Can I leave early?: Asking to leave early signals that you are unreliable and wish to work less, which hurts your chances.

rw: A brief professional summary tied to the job highlights your skills and experience in a way that is relevant to the interviewer.

ww.Say nothing: Saying nothing wastes the chance to introduce yourself and shows poor communication skills, which an interviewer will notice at once.
ww.Share personal secrets about your family: Personal secrets about family and friends are not relevant to the job and are unprofessional to share in an interview.
ww.Read your resume aloud: Reading your resume aloud repeats what the interviewer can already see and does not add anything new about you.

rw: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result, a way to answer by describing what happened, your role, what you did and the outcome.

ww.Start, Talk, Ask, Respond: STAR does not stand for Start, Talk, Ask, Respond; those words do not describe the steps of a structured answer.
ww.Skill, Training, Award, Reference: Skill, Training, Award, Reference is not the STAR method; those words do not outline a story about a past experience.
ww.Sell, Trade, Acquire, Retain: Sell, Trade, Acquire, Retain is not the STAR method; it lists sales terms and says nothing about answering questions.

rw: Contact information should include your name, phone number and a professional email so an employer can reach you easily.

ww.Your password: A password is private and must never appear on a resume, since sharing it could put your accounts at risk.
ww.Your birth date: A birth date is not needed on a resume and can lead to age bias, so it is left off.
ww.Your Social Security number, home addres: A Social Security number and parents' names are private and risky to share, and they do not belong on a resume.

rw: A resume keyword is a term from the job posting that matches your skills, helping applicant tracking systems and recruiters find you.

ww.A font style that makes the page look ne: A font style is about appearance and is not a keyword; a keyword is a term from the job posting.
ww.A margin setting that keeps the text fro: A margin setting is about layout and has nothing to do with matching the wording of the job posting.
ww.A password that lets an employer open th: A password for an employer's site is private login information and is not a resume keyword.

rw: Most entry-level resumes should be one page, which is enough to show the education and skills of a beginner clearly.

ww.Five pages: Five pages is far too long for an entry-level candidate with little experience, and employers will not read that much.
ww.Ten pages: Ten pages is far beyond what any hiring manager would read, especially for a candidate early in a career.
ww.Half a line: Half a line cannot hold contact details, education and skills, so it gives the employer far too little information.

rw: Education is the strongest item for a recent graduate with little experience, so it is listed first on the resume.

ww.Hobbies: Hobbies are of minor interest to employers and, for a recent graduate, should come after education and skills.
ww.Salary history: Salary history should not appear on a resume at all, so it would never be listed first.
ww.References: References are usually given on a separate sheet, if at all, and do not lead a graduate's resume.

rw: Being honest and focusing on what you learned or did, such as courses or volunteering, shows maturity and keeps trust.

ww.Blame others: Blaming others makes you look unprofessional and unwilling to take responsibility, which an interviewer will count against you.
ww.Lie about it: Lying about a gap can be found out and can cost you the job, so honesty is the safer course.
ww.Refuse to answer: Refusing to answer looks evasive and leaves the interviewer to imagine the worst, instead of hearing a clear explanation.

rw: A job fair is an event where several employers meet job seekers to share openings and take applications.

ww.A tax event: A tax event is a government function with no link to employers meeting people who are looking for work.
ww.A county fair: A county fair is a local festival with rides and exhibits, not an event where employers meet job seekers.
ww.A funfair: A funfair is for entertainment, with rides and games, and has no role in hiring or job searching.

rw: Asking for permission is polite and makes sure the person is willing to give you a good reference when called.

ww.Tell them after the application has been: Telling them after the application is sent means they may be caught off guard by a call, so you must ask first.
ww.Pay them: Paying a reference is improper and could cast doubt on their honesty; a reference gives their view freely.
ww.Nothing: Doing nothing risks surprising the person with a call and they may give a poor or unprepared answer.

rw: Salary negotiation is discussing pay and benefits with an employer before accepting a job, so both sides agree on terms.

ww.Skipping pay talk: Skipping pay talk means you may accept less than you could, so it is not negotiation at all.
ww.Refusing to work: Refusing to work is not a negotiation; it ends the discussion rather than seeking agreement on pay.
ww.Demanding a high salary without research: Demanding a high salary without research ignores what others pay, which is unrealistic and unlikely to succeed in a real negotiation.

rw: Giving proper notice and leaving on good terms protects your reputation and keeps the employer as a possible reference.

ww.Insult the boss: Insulting the boss damages relationships and your reputation, which can hurt future references and job chances.
ww.Quit without notice: Quitting without notice leaves the employer in a bind and can harm your reputation and a future reference.
ww.Take company property, such as a laptop: Taking company property is theft, which could lead to legal trouble and ruin your professional reputation.

rw: Two weeks is the usual notice period, giving the employer time to cover your duties or find a replacement.

ww.Two years: Two years is far longer than any normal notice period and would be unreasonable to ask of a worker.
ww.None required ever: Saying none is ever required is incorrect, since giving notice is the professional norm and may be required by contract.
ww.Two hours: Two hours is too short for an employer to plan for your leaving and counts as quitting without proper notice.

rw: A professional email address is based on your name rather than a nickname, which looks serious and is easy for employers to recognize.

ww.A slang phrase: A slang phrase looks unprofessional to employers and does not help them take your application seriously.
ww.A joke nickname: A joke nickname may amuse friends but makes a poor impression on an employer reading your resume.
ww.An emoji address: An emoji address is not professional and may not even work in email, so employers would not take it seriously.

rw: LinkedIn is mainly used for professional networking and job searching, letting users share their work history and meet employers.

ww.Streaming music: Streaming music is done on audio services, not on LinkedIn, which is built for professional connections and careers.
ww.Online gaming: Online gaming is done on game platforms, which are separate from LinkedIn, a site for careers and contacts.
ww.Sharing vacation photos with friends and: Sharing vacation photos is what personal social media is for; LinkedIn is mainly for professional contacts and job searching.

rw: Errors can create a poor impression of your care and attention, so proofreading before you send protects your chances.

ww.Employers ignore errors, since they focu: Employers do notice errors and may reject careless applicants, so claiming they ignore mistakes is false.
ww.It is unnecessary: Proofreading is necessary, because skipping it can leave mistakes that make you look careless to an employer.
ww.Errors make it better: Errors do not improve a resume; they make it look sloppy and can lead to rejection.

rw: Revenue is 200 x $8 = $1,600, and subtracting the $1,200 total costs leaves a profit of $400.

ww.$1,200, which is the total cost of runni: $1,200 is the total cost of running the shop, not the profit; profit is the revenue minus that amount, which is $400.
ww.$2,800, found by adding the revenue to t: $2,800 adds revenue to costs ($1,600 + $1,200), but costs must be subtracted from revenue to find profit.
ww.$1,600, which is the total revenue befor: $1,600 is the total revenue of 200 mugs at $8, which is the figure before the $1,200 of costs is taken away.

rw: Each loaf contributes $3 minus $1 = $2 toward fixed costs, so the break-even is $500 / $2 = 250 loaves.

ww.500 loaves, found by dividing the fixed: 500 loaves divides fixed costs by the $1 cost, but each loaf earns $2 toward fixed costs, so fewer are needed.
ww.167 loaves, found by dividing the fixed: 167 loaves divides $500 by the $3 price, but break-even must use the $2 contribution per loaf, not the price.
ww.1,500 loaves, found by multiplying the f: 1,500 loaves multiplies the fixed costs by the price, but break-even is found by dividing, using the contribution of $2.

rw: Fuel rises and falls with the amount of mowing done, so it is a variable cost for the lawn-care company.

ww.The salary of the manager who runs the w: A manager's salary is paid all year whatever the number of lawns cut, so it is a fixed cost, not variable.
ww.The monthly lease payment on the office: The monthly office lease stays the same however many lawns are mowed, so it is a fixed cost.
ww.The yearly insurance premium paid on the: Yearly insurance on trucks and equipment is a set amount no matter how much work is done, so it is fixed.

rw: Monthly rent stays the same however many meals are served, which is what makes it a fixed cost.

ww.The cost of the ingredients used in each: Ingredients used in each meal rise with the number of meals served, so they are a variable cost.
ww.The cost of the takeout boxes used for o: Takeout boxes are used up in proportion to the number of takeout orders, so their cost is variable.
ww.The extra hourly wages of part-time staf: Extra wages for a busy weekend are added only when trade is heavy, so they change with output and are variable.

rw: Revenue minus expenses is $90,000 - $95,000 = -$5,000, so expenses are higher and the company has a loss of $5,000.

ww.A profit of $5,000, because the larger f: Profit needs revenue above expenses, but $90,000 is less than $95,000, so the larger figure is the expenses and the result is a loss.
ww.Break-even, because the revenue and the: Break-even needs revenue to equal expenses exactly, and $90,000 does not equal $95,000, so there is a shortfall.
ww.A profit of $185,000, found by adding th: Adding revenue and expenses to get $185,000 is meaningless; profit comes from subtracting expenses from revenue.

rw: Fifty percent of $40 is $20, and adding it to the $40 cost gives a selling price of $60.

map.$90, which adds the full cost to the cos: $90, which adds fifty dollars to the cost instead of half of the cost

ww.$50, which adds only ten dollars to the: $50 adds only $10, which is 25% of $40, but a 50% markup adds $20 to the cost.
ww.$20, which is the amount of the markup a: $20 is the markup amount only; the selling price must include the original $40 cost as well.
ww.$90, which adds fifty dollars to the cos: $90 adds fifty dollars to the cost, but 50 percent of $40 is $20, so the price is $60.

rw: Profit margin is net profit divided by revenue, so $5,000 / $50,000 = 0.10, or 10 percent.

map.45 percent, found by subtracting the pro: 45 percent, found by halving the 90 percent expense share of revenue

ww.1 percent, found by moving the decimal o: 1 percent puts the decimal point too far; $5,000 / $50,000 = 0.10, which is 10 percent.
ww.90 percent, found by dividing the expens: 90 percent is expenses divided by revenue ($45,000 / $50,000), which is the cost share and not the profit share.
ww.45 percent, found by halving the 90 perc: 45 percent has no basis here; halving the 90 percent expense share is not a margin, and $5,000 / $50,000 gives 10 percent.

rw: Revenue is price times units, so a business must check whether the higher price outweighs the lost sales and whether profit rose or fell.

ww.Only the number of units, because the pr: Price has a direct effect on revenue, so looking only at units sold ignores that revenue equals price times quantity.
ww.Nothing, because fewer units always mean: Fewer units do not always mean a bigger profit, because revenue may fall by more than costs do.
ww.Nothing, because a higher price always m: A higher price does not guarantee more profit, since sales may fall so far that total revenue drops.

rw: Break-even is the sales level where total revenue equals total costs, so the business neither makes a profit nor suffers a loss.

ww.The sales level at which the business mu: The business does not have to close at break-even, since revenue already covers its costs, including staff wages.
ww.The sales level at which the profit of t: Profit is not at its highest at break-even; profit there is zero, and it grows only as sales rise beyond that point.
ww.The sales level at which the business ha: At break-even the business has customers and earns revenue; it simply earns exactly enough to cover its costs.

rw: Tracking costs lets a business set prices that cover its costs and still leave a profit, which keeps it running.

ww.To give the owner a reason to stop selli: Tracking costs helps owners find which goods to promote and does not give a reason to stop selling goods customers want.
ww.To avoid paying any tax on the profit th: Costs are tracked to price correctly, not to dodge taxes; trying to avoid all tax on profit would be illegal.
ww.To make the business look larger to bank: Making a business look larger to banks is misleading; costs are tracked to run the firm well, not to deceive lenders.

rw: Extra cost is the change in cost over the change in output: $2,000 / 500 units = $4 per added unit.

ww.$8, found by dividing the new total cost: $8 divides the new total cost by the units at the end ($12,000 / 1,500), which is average cost, not extra cost.
ww.$10, found by dividing the original tota: $10 divides the original cost by the starting units ($10,000 / 1,000), which gives the earlier average cost, not marginal.
ww.$2, found by dividing the extra cost by: $2 divides the extra cost by the 1,000 original units; the divisor must be the 500 added units, which gives $4.

rw: Cutting costs without lowering quality keeps revenue the same while expenses shrink, so profit rises.

ww.Raising its costs while keeping the same: Higher costs with the same prices and sales cut the gap between revenue and costs, which lowers profit.
ww.Lowering its prices below its cost of ma: Pricing below cost means each sale loses money, so profit falls rather than rises.
ww.Spending money on a product that custome: Money spent on a product nobody wants adds cost without adding revenue, so profit falls.

rw: Profit is earnings minus costs, so $3,000 minus $1,800 leaves $1,200 for the freelancer that month.

ww.$4,800, found by adding together the ear: $4,800 adds the earnings to the costs, but profit is earnings minus costs, so costs must be subtracted.
ww.$1,800, which is the amount spent on cos: $1,800 is the amount spent on costs and not what is left over; the profit is $3,000 minus $1,800.
ww.$3,000, which is the earnings figure bef: $3,000 is the earnings before costs were taken out; subtracting the $1,800 of costs leaves a profit of $1,200.

rw: A loss leader is a product sold at a low price, even at a loss, to attract customers who then buy other goods.

ww.A product that earns the highest profit: A loss leader is not the highest-profit product; it is priced low to draw shoppers, so its own profit is small or negative.
ww.A product sold only to employees at a de: A product sold only to staff at a discount is an employee perk, not a pricing tactic meant to attract shoppers.
ww.A product that the firm makes at a loss: A loss leader is advertised to bring shoppers in, so hiding it from customers would defeat its whole purpose.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, here the rent income lost by using the building as a shop.

ww.The tax that the business paid on its pr: Tax paid on profits is an actual payment of money, an explicit cost, not the value of a choice given up.
ww.The wages paid to the staff for the hour: Wages paid to staff are an explicit cost already paid out of the firm's funds, not an income given up.
ww.The price paid for the supplies used up: The price paid for supplies is an out-of-pocket expense, not the value of the next best use of resources.

rw: Lowering a price on an item that isn't selling attracts buyers and clears stock, freeing space and cash for other goods.

ww.To increase the profit on each unit, sin: Lower prices do not always bring a higher margin per unit; they usually reduce the margin, offset by sales volume.
ww.To stop customers from buying any items: Cutting a price is meant to encourage buying, not stop customers from buying anything for a while.
ww.To show customers that the quality of th: Lowering a price does not show that quality has fallen; stores cut prices mainly to move unsold goods.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, so studying costs the student the $90 forgone from working.

ww.Nothing, because studying is free and th: Studying has a cost even without cash paid, because the student gives up the $90 that working would have earned.
ww.The price of the textbook that the stude: A textbook the student already owns is a sunk cost, not the value of the alternative forgone by studying.
ww.The grade the student will get on the ex: The grade is a benefit of studying, not what is given up; opportunity cost is the $90 not earned.

rw: With supply unchanged, higher demand creates a shortage at the old price, so competing buyers push the price up.

ww.The price falls to zero because buyers h: Prices do not fall to zero when demand rises; more buyers competing for the same supply push prices up.
ww.The price stays the same because supply: Price does not stay the same, because rising demand against unchanged supply creates a shortage that bids prices up.
ww.The price tends to fall because more buy: More buyers do not create a larger supply; supply is unchanged, so higher demand tends to raise the price.
